title: A Reply to Makelov et al. (2023)'s "Interpretability Illusion" Arguments

data.title: A Reply to Makelov et al. (2023)’s “Interpretability Illusion” Arguments
data.research_question: Are the phenomena Makelov et al. (2023) call “interpretability illusions” genuine failures of distributed interchange interventions/DAS, or artifacts of their training and evaluation paradigms?

models_and_data.quote: We use the GPT-2 model Small checkpoint from HuggingFace.

models_and_data.item: IOI dataset generation scripts from Makelov et al.
models_and_data.quote: We use the dataset generation scripts from the publicly released code of Makelov et al. (2023).
The toy example involves a simple linear neural network f (x) = (xW1⊺ )W2 where W1 = [1, 0, 1]⊺ and W2 = [0, 2, 1]⊺.

protocol.step: Decompose the DAS direction into nullspace and rowspace components
protocol.quote: Makelov et al. decompose v into two orthogonal parts as,

protocol.step: Define an illusion as a much smaller causal effect for the rowspace-only intervention
protocol.quote: an “illusion” arises if the causal effect of intervening on vr is much smaller than v towards the desired goal

protocol.step: Train a single DAS direction on base-source pairs
protocol.quote: To train a single DAS direction, we sample 200 pairs of base and source example pairs.

protocol.step: Evaluate alignment with interchange intervention accuracy
protocol.quote: We use IIA as our evaluation metric.
we perform Leave-One-Out (LOO) alignment: we align with concatenated head representations by leaving one head out at a time.

protocol.step: Use Boundless DAS as a variable-dimensionality variant
protocol.quote: we also experimented with Boundless DAS (Wu et al., 2023), a variant of DAS that does not assume a fixed dimensionality for the DAS subspace.

metrics.name: Interchange intervention accuracy (IIA)
metrics.definition: Percentage of counterfactual predictions matched under interchange interventions between the high-level causal model and the neural model.
metrics.quote: Interchange intervention accuracy (IIA) is the percentage of counterfactual predictions matched under interchange interventions between the high-level causal model and the neural model.

metrics.name: Fractional logit difference decrease (FLDD)
metrics.definition: Fractional logit difference between the IO and S tokens before and after the intervention.
metrics.quote: FLDD measures a frac- tional logit difference between the IO and S (i.e., incorrect output token) tokens before and after the intervention

metrics.name: Task accuracy
metrics.definition: Model task performance on the IOI task.
metrics.quote: GPT-2 can achieve a task performance of 91.6%.

metrics.name: Illusion effect
metrics.definition: Difference in causal effect between intervening on v and vr alone.
metrics.quote: I LLUSION E FFECT represents the difference in causal effect between intervening on v and vr alone.

key_results.claim: A direction Makelov et al. call non-illusory still has an illusion effect; rowspace-only intervention retains only 20% of the causal effect.
key_results.quote: This shows the causal effect by intervening with vr alone greatly diminishes by only retaining 20% of the causal effect when intervening on v.

key_results.claim: Makelov et al. report very low IIA for MLP intervention locations, far below GPT-2 task performance.
key_results.quote: Makelov et al. (2023) end up with an IIA ranging from 0.0% to 4.2% for intervention locations in MLP layers

key_results.claim: DAS finds name-position information in the main residual stream at the 8th layer but much less in MLP activations.
key_results.quote: The learned DAS direction achieves an IIA of 70% with the main residual stream (vblock out ) and an IIA of 4% with the MLP activations (vmlp act )

key_results.claim: At the 8th layer, attention output and block output carry substantial name-position information.
key_results.quote: the attention output stream (vattn out ) reaches about 48% IIA, and the resulting block output stream reaches about 69% IIA.

key_results.claim: Head 6 alone reaches 0% IIA and with head 10 remains below 20%, supporting distributed head processing.
key_results.quote: head 6 alone reaches 0% IIA, and it reaches less than 20% when considered together with head 10

key_results.claim: DAS finds a new attention-value-output alignment with 13% IIA where vanilla interchange intervention is 0%.
key_results.quote: DAS finds new alignments in the attention value output stream with an IIA of 13% where the vanilla interchange intervention flats out with a 0% IIA.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: IIA has limitations as an interpretability measure.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: Although IIA has limitations (as outlined in Geiger et al. 2023; Wu et al. 2023), it offers an intuitive measure

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: FLDD can be misleading because it is a ratio of log-likelihoods.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: Because FLDD is based on a ratio of log-likelihoods, it can be brought arbitrarily close to 100% with no effect whatsoever on counterfactual behavior.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: DAS assumes a fixed-size linear subspace, which may not fit binary variables.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: DAS assumes a fixed-size linear subspace; however, a binary variable may not always fit within a linear subspace of a single dimension.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: Activation-only analysis cannot support strong causal claims.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: analysis solely based on activations cannot support strong causal claims about model structures.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: The factual-recall DAS setup can overfit a single fact pair.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: the current experimental setup also entails that the learned DAS direction overfits the single pair of facts seen during training.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: Complex models may admit multiple distinct fully correct causal abstractions.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: for sufficiently complex models, there are still likely to be multiple distinct fully correct abstractions.

threats_not_stated_by_authors: The paper studies GPT-2 Small/XL and a toy linear network, not Gemma 4 E2B or its KV-shared layers 15-34.
The nullspace/rowspace analysis is specific to MLP down-projection weights and does not directly address KV-shared attention layers or per-layer embeddings.
IIA and FLDD are behavioral metrics and may miss internal mechanisms such as induction heads or factual-recall circuits.
Single DAS directions per task/layer may underrepresent distributed representations and may not generalize across templates, names, or facts.
The paper does not test activation patching, logit lens, induction-head tracing, or factual-recall tracing on Gemma 4 E2B.
CPU feasibility and scaling to large models are not analyzed.
The critique is conceptual and empirical on IOI/factual recall; it does not establish whether similar “illusions” occur in KV-shared architectures.
data.relevance_to_lab: Relevant as a caution about nullspace/rowspace artifacts in activation patching and DAS, but it studies GPT-2/toy models rather than Gemma 4 E2B KV-shared layers, per-layer embeddings, logit lens, induction heads, or CPU tracing.

data.title: A Reply to Makelov et al. (2023)’s “Interpretability Illusion” Arguments
data.research_question: Do Makelov et al.’s “interpretability illusions” show that distributed or subspace interchange interventions are invalid, and are their empirical demonstrations artifacts of experimental design?

models_and_data.item: A three-hidden-unit linear toy network implementing a copy function.
models_and_data.quote: The toy example involves a simple linear neural network f (x) = (xW1⊺ )W2 where W1 = [1, 0, 1]⊺ and W2 = [0, 2, 1]⊺ .

models_and_data.item: GPT-2 Small checkpoint used for the paper’s IOI experiments.
models_and_data.quote: We use the GPT-2 model Small checkpoint from HuggingFace.

models_and_data.item: IOI data for aligning a binary name-position variable with distributed representations.
models_and_data.quote: Following Makelov et al. (2023), we learn a single DAS direction to localize the name position in the IOI task.

models_and_data.item: Paired IOI data for learning representations of the correct indirect-object name.
models_and_data.quote: To find the IO name representations, we sample 200 pairs of base and source randomly and have the correct counterfactual label to be the source IO name.

models_and_data.item: Factual-recall experimental setup reviewed from Makelov et al.
models_and_data.quote: Makelov et al. (2023) also try to replicate their finding of “illusion” in the factual recall task as in their Section 6.1 (p. 20).

models_and_data.item: Alpaca simple in-context reasoning task used as an external IIA comparison.
models_and_data.quote: For example, in the study of how Alpaca solves a simple reasoning task in context (Wu et al., 2023), we see IIA values around 85% even in ambitious, out-of-domain evaluations.

protocol.step: Intervene on the activation induced by example A using the activation induced by example B along a learned subspace v.
protocol.quote: Intervening on activations created by A with B in the subspace spanned by v can be expressed as,

protocol.step: Decompose the intervention direction into orthogonal nullspace and rowspace components relative to the MLP down-projection matrix.
protocol.quote: Makelov et al. decompose v into two orthogonal parts as,

protocol.step: Compare the causal effect of intervening on the full direction with the effect of intervening only on its rowspace component.
protocol.quote: the main experiments that Makelov et al. designed is to compare the causal effect on model predictions of intervening on v with intervening on vr alone

protocol.step: Evaluate the toy example using concrete inputs and compare full-subspace and rowspace-only outputs.
protocol.quote: intervening along v will result in an output of 5, and intervening along vr will result in an output of 5 − 0.8 × (5 − 1) = 1.8 which is much lower

protocol.step: Learn a single DAS direction for the IOI name-position variable and test it at seven intervention locations.
protocol.quote: We try seven intervention locations to find the causal variable as annotated in Figure 1.

protocol.step: Train the DAS direction with Adam using the reported learning rate, epochs, and batch size.
protocol.quote: We use the Adam optimizer (Kingma & Ba, 2015) with an initial learning rate of 0.01 for an epoch number of 10 with a batch size of 20.

protocol.step: Rank attention heads by leave-one-out IIA loss and then build cumulative head representations in that order.
protocol.quote: We then rank the IIA drops across heads from the highest (i.e., leaving this head out results in the biggest loss in IIA) to the lowest based on LOO experiments.

protocol.step: Compare vanilla interchange interventions with DAS when locating the correct IO-name representation.
protocol.quote: To find the IO token representation, we use vanilla interchange interventions (Geiger et al., 2021) as well as DAS.

metrics.name: Illusion Effect
metrics.definition: The difference in downstream causal effect between intervening along the full subspace direction v and intervening along its rowspace component alone.
metrics.quote: Recall that I LLUSION E FFECT represents the difference in causal effect between intervening on v and vr alone.

metrics.name: Interchange Intervention Accuracy (IIA)
metrics.definition: The percentage of counterfactual predictions matched under interchange interventions between a high-level causal model and the neural model.
metrics.quote: Interchange intervention accuracy (IIA) is the percentage of counterfactual predictions matched under interchange interventions between the high-level causal model and the neural model.

metrics.name: Fractional Logit Difference Decrease (FLDD)
metrics.definition: The fractional change in the logit difference between the correct IO token and incorrect S token before and after an intervention.
metrics.quote: FLDD measures a fractional logit difference between the IO and S (i.e., incorrect output token) tokens before and after the intervention, as described in Equation 4 in the paper.

metrics.name: Task accuracy
metrics.definition: The proportion of examples on which GPT-2 produces the correct task answer.
metrics.quote: The GPT-2 model achieves 96% task accuracy.

metrics.name: Leave-One-Out head IIA
metrics.definition: IIA obtained with a concatenated head representation while omitting one attention head at a time.
metrics.quote: The top panel shows IIA when aligning with a concatenated representation of all heads in the 8th layer by leaving one head out at a time.

metrics.name: Cumulative-head IIA
metrics.definition: IIA obtained by cumulatively concatenating heads in descending order of leave-one-out IIA loss.
metrics.quote: The bottom panel shows IIA when aligning with cumulated head representations by starting from the head resulting in the largest drop in the top panel

key_results.claim: The authors reject the “illusion” label and interpret the effects as discoveries about distributed representations.
key_results.quote: These are simply discoveries about distributed representations.

key_results.claim: In the toy example, the direction identified as non-illusory produces an illusion effect, and rowspace-only intervention retains only 20% of the full intervention’s causal effect.
key_results.quote: This shows the causal effect by intervening with vr alone greatly diminishes by only retaining 20% of the causal effect when intervening on v.

key_results.claim: For IOI name-position information, DAS aligns strongly with the main residual stream but weakly with MLP activations.
key_results.quote: The learned DAS direction achieves an IIA of 70% with the main residual stream (vblock out ) and an IIA of 4% with the MLP activations (vmlp act )

key_results.claim: Name-position information emerges prominently through the self-attention block at the 8th layer.
key_results.quote: of the 8th layer (i.e., the block output stream of the previous layer) reaches about 11% IIA, the attention output stream (vattn out ) reaches about 48% IIA, and the resulting block output stream reaches about 69% IIA.

key_results.claim: Name-position information is distributed across attention heads: leaving heads 6 and 10 out causes the largest IIA losses, while head 6 alone reaches 0% IIA and remains below 20% when paired with head 10.
key_results.quote: Our results show that head 6 alone reaches 0% IIA, and it reaches less than 20% when considered together with head 10 as shown in the bottom panel of Figure 4.

key_results.claim: DAS finds an attention-value alignment for the correct IO name that vanilla interchange intervention misses.
key_results.quote: Comparing results from DAS with vanilla interchange intervention, we find that DAS finds new alignments in the attention value output stream with an IIA of 13% where the vanilla interchange intervention flats out with a 0% IIA.

key_results.claim: Boundless DAS outperforms standard DAS when aligning the correct IO-name variable.
key_results.quote: However, it demonstrates superior performance in alignment with the correct IO name.

key_results.claim: The correct IO-name representation appears to emerge beginning at the 9th layer.
key_results.quote: As shown in Figure 6, the correct IO token seems to emerge starting from the 9th layer.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: The authors judge the empirical evidence provided by Makelov et al. to be weak.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: Our view is that the evidence provided in favor of this claim is not strong.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: IIA has acknowledged limitations as a measure of interpretability.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: Although IIA has limitations (as outlined in Geiger et al. 2023; Wu et al., 2023), it offers an intuitive measure for gauging the interpretability of a neural model

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: FLDD can approach 100% without producing any counterfactual behavioral change.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: Because FLDD is based on a ratio of log-likelihoods, it can be brought arbitrarily close to 100% with no effect whatsoever on counterfactual behavior.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: Activation-distribution analysis alone cannot justify strong causal claims.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: We thus argue that analysis solely based on activations cannot support strong causal claims about model structures.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: The single-pair factual-recall DAS experiment aligns with an uninteresting dummy causal model.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: the learned DAS direction aligns the neural network with an uninteresting high-level causal model: a dummy model that always returns the answer of the seen source example.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: The single-pair factual-recall DAS setup overfits the facts used for training.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: the current experimental setup also entails that the learned DAS direction overfits the single pair of facts seen during training.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: The learned factual-recall directions are unlikely to generalize beyond the observed facts.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: As a result, their directions would likely not generalize to any other facts except the ones it is trained on.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: Cumulative-head results are sensitive to the ordering of heads.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: In practice, given the scale of the dataset and the magnitude of IIAs, we observe variance in results as the order changes.

threats_not_stated_by_authors: The experiments use GPT-2 Small and review GPT-2-XL, so the reported geometry and layer-wise findings are not validated on Gemma 4 E2B.
KV sharing, layers 15–34, and per-layer embedding intervention sites are not tested, leaving transfer to the lab’s architecture unknown.
Training is reported on a single 12G Nvidia GPU, leaving CPU-only feasibility and memory scaling for Gemma-scale models unaddressed.
No induction-head circuit is evaluated, so IOI name-mover findings cannot establish induction-head behavior in Gemma.
Factual recall is discussed primarily as a critique of prior work rather than rerun with a modern experimental design, leaving little direct factual-recall tracing evidence.
No confidence intervals, significance tests, or seed-level uncertainty are reported for most IIA comparisons; only ordering variance is noted.
The connection between head importance and DAS weight sparsity is primarily qualitative rather than supported by a reported statistical analysis.
Exact environment and dependency versions for the external code and dataset-generation scripts are not specified in the provided text, creating reproducibility risk across library revisions.
data.relevance_to_lab: The paper is directly relevant as a methodological warning and template for activation-patching work: it shows why full-subspace versus rowspace-only patches should be compared, argues that nonorthogonality to downstream nullspaces can reflect distributed structure rather than failed explanation, and recommends IIA, logit-difference or KL-style checks, and head-wise leave-one-out and cumulative tracing. The lab can adapt these procedures to Gemma 4 E2B by testing per-layer embeddings and intervention sites across KV-shared layers 15–34, but the paper provides no Gemma-specific, induction-head, CPU-feasibility, or modern factual-recall validation.
